Malta Places to Stay

This 300-Year-Old Maltese Mansion Just Became One of the Island's Most Romantic Stays

September 3, 2026
Words by Heidi Mitchell
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 12:35
Instaread

Casa Bonavita, a rescued 18th-century estate in the residential outskirts of Valletta, has reopened as a 17-room boutique hotel with serious design pedigree

Malta packs Roman ruins, Arab-influenced hill towns, its baroque capital of Valletta and some of the clearest, bluest water in the Mediterranean onto three tiny islands you can cross in less than an hour. Across millennia, the country had waves of Phoenician, Arab, Sicilian, Spanish, and British rule, and that layered history shows up everywhere, from the language to the architecture to the food. It’s also, refreshingly, still under-visited by the design crowd – which is exactly the gap Casa Bonavita is stepping into.

Casa Bonavita is the passion project of Suzanne and Christopher Sharp, the couple behind The Rug Company, who stumbled on the crumbling circa-1715 mansion in the inland village of Attard back in 2010. They spent 15 years slowly restoring it, first into a family home, and then later – as their retirement project – into a boutique hotel, with help from their antiques-dealer son and ceramicist daughter. For readers chasing places with real provenance, that’s the whole appeal.
The interiors of Casa Bonavita are a curation of tactile, bohemian objects | Photos by Julian Vassallo

What’s the vibe?


Casa Bonavita leans heavily into faded aristocratic grandeur: frescoed 19th-century ceilings, Aubusson carpets, Genoese furniture, and a jumble of Mediterranean art sourced on what the Sharps describe as several very enjoyable shopping trips. That curation gives the whole place the feeling of a lived-in palazzo rather than some soulless five-star hotel. The vibe is cosy (see: the backgammon patio) and collected over years rather than staged. An aesthete will swoon.

The Sharps kept the house’s original bones as a home largely intact – tearing down false ceilings to reveal the original arches, for example – while adding two adjacent buildings to the retreat.

And the setting adds to that atmosphere. Attard sits between Valletta and the old island capital of Mdina, and the hotel backs onto sprawling walled gardens thick with bougainvillea and orange blossom – a genuine surprise behind an unassuming limestone facade. It’s an inland retreat, so anyone wanting sea views or a beach five minutes away should look elsewhere; you’ll need a car or taxi to reach the coast or any of Malta’s attractions. But you could just stay here and live like a local for a couple of magical days.

The hotel has 17 rooms | Photo by Boz Gagovski

What are the rooms like?


Just 17 rooms across the main house and separate annexes keep things intimate. Seven of the best quarters occupy the original building, including one former “salone nobile” suite with marble-effect wallpaper and a classic Maltese balcony. Expect suzani textiles, Karabagh rugs (they did run a massive textile company, after all), and ceramic lamps from the family’s own Villa Bologna Pottery workshop nearby. Many rooms have private balconies or terraces, and breakfast can be taken in-room for guests who want to disappear entirely.

Groups and families should consider booking the Dower’s House. Its five bedrooms, including one superior room and two two-bedroom suites, are linked by connecting balconies, so if you book it out in its own right, you effectively get a villa-within-a-hotel experience – private, but with the main house’s kitchen, gardens, and spa on tap.

Food, drink and everything else


The dining room, hand-painted to recreate its former life as a courtyard garden, and a shady pergola for al fresco meals are both reasons enough to linger over lunch (and are open to non-resident guests).

The bar, with its panelled scenes inspired by an 18th-century Maltese painter, has chartreuse velvet sofas and 1960s bamboo chairs to keep things unstuffy, while a menu of club sandwiches and burgers seals the deal. There’s also a subterranean spa with two pools and Sicilian-tiled doors, for days you don’t leave the grounds at all.
Advertisement
The hotel’s walled garden features classical motifs | Photo by Julian Vassallo

Things I should know


The house’s original Sicilian-tiled kitchen, fitted out with a Lacanche range, hasn’t been closed off into some staff-only production line, meaning guests are welcome to wander in. Come down for a croissant and coffee before breakfast service officially starts, help yourself to berries and yoghurt mid-morning, or raid it for a midnight snack after one too many Negronis in the garden. It’s a small detail, but it sets the tone for the whole property: This is your house, at least for the night.

What’s the dress code?


Casual, but make it intentional. This is a design-literate crowd, not a backpacker one, so think beach chic: linen shirts, good sandals, and a decent sundress or billowy button-down for dinner over resort wear or anything overly polished. Straw hats are de rigueur.
Guests are able to wander through the hotel kitchen as they please | Photos by Boz Gagovski

What’s the crowd like?


Design-driven travellers who know Malta well enough to avoid sleeping in Valletta, where the backpackers and package tourists tend to cluster. This is a guest list that’ll clock the inspiration of Egyptian mashrabiya woodwork in the balconies and the Maltese slip-casting ceramics on property; they’re here as much for the architecture and gardens as the pool, and more likely to spend an evening playing board games in a shaded corner than out looking for a club.

What’s nearby?


Villa Bologna Pottery, the workshop run by the Sharps’ daughter Sophie Edwards and the source of much of the hotel’s ceramics, is a short drive away and worth the detour for a proper piece to bring home. It also has a wonderful Italian restaurant.

For an evening out, take a taxi to Mdina, Malta’s old walled capital, about 10 minutes from Attard. Nicknamed the Silent City, it’s a fortified medieval town of narrow limestone lanes and baroque palazzi that’s almost empty once the day-trippers clear out, which makes for one of the more atmospheric walks on the island.

Wander to Bastion Square for the view over the countryside toward the sea, or duck into St Paul’s Cathedral if it's open. Bring a light layer, since the walls keep in a breeze, even on balmy summer evenings.
Advertisement
The 18th-century Maltese mansion was restored over 15 years | Photos by Boz Gagovski

Is it worth it?


The trade-off here is soul versus location. Seventeen rooms means this will book out fast once word spreads, and rooms cost more than many of the standard spots in Malta. For design-minded travellers who are keen to witness the country’s layered history told through an actual family home, and for families or groups who can bag the Dower’s House outright, Casa Bonavita looks like the rare new opening worth planning a trip around – and a solid excuse to give Malta more than a day of your Mediterranean itinerary.

How much does it cost?


Rooms from £623; casabonavita.com
